article.title: Single-Payer Healthcare Deadlock
article.author: Larry Gross
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. California would seem to be the most likely state to enact a true single-payer healthcare program [SP]. After all, SP is favored by majorities, including Republicans. However, successive legislative efforts to pass CalCare, the SP plan sponsored by the California Nurses Association [CNA], have been killed by Democratic leaders before they could come to a vote. Actually, that’s not quite true: SP bills were passed by the CA legislature twice, when Republican governor Arnold Schwarzenegger promised to veto them. When Democrat Gavin Newsom, who ran on a SP platform and was supported by CNA, was elected, he made sure that no SP bill ever reached his desk. The reason for the repeated failure of SP legislation is not a mystery: the immense wealth of the health insurance complex gives them an unsurmountable advantage in determining the actions of Democratic politicians in the legislature and the governor’s office. To put it simply, when serious interests are at stake, legislators can be bribed or they can be scared. The SP forces are woefully outmatched financially, and have not yet been able to inspire the sort of public outrage that would effectively scare enough legislators. Thus, it’s not surprising that SP advocates are once again considering the option of a ballot measure that would enshrine healthcare as a right, and SP as the vehicle, in the California constitution. In 1994 CA voters defeated Proposition 186, which would have established a universal, publicly financed, single-payer health care system in California, effectively eliminating private health insurance as the principal means of paying for medical care. There were numerous reasons that effort failed, among them the timing: the Clinton health reform initiative collapsed in Congress in September 1994, just weeks before the California election. But among the major reasons the proposition failed was the enormous financial advantage of the opponents, who outspent proponents $9 million to $2.7 million. Related: Socialist Health Care Organizers Exit DSA The opposition concentrated on three arguments: higher taxes, increased government control of medical decisions, and uncertainty about the quality and availability of care under a completely reorganized system. More than 30 years later, the public is much more sophisticated about the realities of health care and certainly much more aware of the disadvantage of the profit-centered system of private health insurance, which have only become more acute with the invasion of the health sphere by private equity vultures. Any campaign to pass a SP proposition would once again have to counter the false claims that SP would cost citizens more, and would have to show business owners, as well as union members and leaders, how they would benefit by taking health insurance costs off the benefit bargaining table. But these are more achievable goals today, after decades of insurance company over-reach and greed, and with a public increasingly angered and anguished by the rising costs and diminishing benefits of private insurance. Now that the next governor will be Xavier Beccera, who has made it clear that he doesn’t support SP, there’s no point in resurrecting a doomed-to-fail legislative campaign. So what’s to prevent the advocates of SP from embarking on a ballot measure campaign? The standard answer, of course, is the enormous amount of money that would be needed, even assuming a successful grassroots campaign could be organized, with the necessary enthusiastic participation of a broad coalition of labor and community organizations. It’s the money, stupid, is the familiar refrain one hears when the topic is raised. But there might be an answer to that conversation stopper. What if there was a billionaire around who was strongly and sincerely dedicated to achieving SP healthcare in California, and was easily able to seed a ballot measure campaign with the millions needed to launch and sustain the effort ? There just might be. Tom Steyer ran in the recent gubernatorial primary on a platform that was unambiguous about his [newly acquired] support for SP: Tom knows quality health care is a right, not a privilege – and that there’s too much profit, and not enough health care, in our health care system. That’s why he’s been endorsed by the California Nurses Association , and progressive single payer health care champions like Congressman Ro Khanna and Representative Ash Kalra, the author of Cal-Care. Tom believes strongly that the only way we’ll reduce health care costs, expand coverage, and promote public health when it is under attack from the Trump administration is through a single-payer system . And he is committed to getting California there. As the largest and most powerful state, California will set an example for the rest of the United States to follow. Tom Steyer spent a reported $220 million on his unsuccessful campaign for the gubernatorial nomination, which would make spending, say, $22 million on a single-payer ballot measure a real bargain. This is the moment for the advocates of SP in California, including the California Nurses Association, to challenge Tom Steyer to put his money where his campaign platform was, and to provide the necessary funding to launch a broad-based coalition to put a true SP measure on the ballot in 2028.
